questions.questionText: According to the explanation, what condition triggers a merge conflict when multiple collaborators work on the same file?
options: A collaborator pushes changes without first pulling the latest version
One collaborator deletes a file while another edits it
Two collaborators edit different files in the repository
Two collaborators edit the same part of the file
questions.correctAnswer: Two collaborators edit the same part of the file
questions.explanation: A merge conflict occurs when two people make changes to the same part of the code, and Git cannot determine which version to keep automatically.

questions.questionText: Collaborator 2 attempted to push changes to README.md but received a merge conflict because collaborator 1 had added a line at the same location. Which sequence of Git commands correctly resolves the conflict and completes the push?
options: git merge --abort; edit README.md; git add README.md; git commit -m "Abort merge"; git push
git fetch; git rebase origin/feature-abc; edit README.md; git add README.md; git rebase --continue; git push
git pull; edit README.md to resolve conflicts; git add README.md; git commit -m "Merge conflict resolved"; git push
git fetch; git merge origin/feature-abc; edit README.md to resolve conflicts; git add README.md; git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"; git push
questions.correctAnswer: git pull; edit README.md to resolve conflicts; git add README.md; git commit -m "Merge conflict resolved"; git push
questions.explanation: When a push fails due to upstream changes, the standard remedy is to run 'git pull', which fetches the remote changes and attempts to merge them. The merge will produce conflict markers in README.md. After manually editing the file to resolve the conflict, the file must be staged with 'git add', committed, and then pushed again. The other options either abort the merge or use rebase without completing the conflict resolution, which would not correctly finish the scenario described.
